name: information-architecture
description: Use when structuring and validating product content and labels.
---

# Information Architecture

Organize content around user needs and product context. Treat any proposed taxonomy as a hypothesis until validated with representative users or behavior.

## Workflow
1. Clarify users, key tasks, content inventory, constraints, platform, and existing terminology. Separate supplied evidence from assumptions.
2. Identify the structural question: grouping, labels, hierarchy, cross-links, or findability. Draft a small number of plausible structures and explain tradeoffs.
3. Choose a method that answers the question: start with a content audit when inventory or ownership is incomplete; use an open/closed/hybrid card sort for grouping or labels, a tree test for findability in a proposed hierarchy, and task observation for contextual routes. If the inventory is already reliable, begin with the method that matches the largest unresolved question. Do not use a card sort to claim a structure is findable or a tree test to claim the wording is preferred.
4. State participant profile, task/sample limitations, success measure, and unresolved bias before interpreting any supplied results. Never invent research outcomes or claim statistical certainty from anecdotal data.
5. Recommend the next validation step and record what would change the taxonomy. Keep navigation polish separate from the underlying grouping decision.

For method selection and evidence labels, read `references/ia-methods.md`. Hand off menu layout to `navigation-controls` and broader discovery to `ux-discovery`.

# Information architecture methods

## Match method to question

| Question | Useful method | What it can support |
|---|---|---|
| What content exists and what is duplicated or missing? | Content inventory/audit | A documented inventory and candidate cleanup |
| How do people group topics or interpret labels? | Card sorting (open, closed, or hybrid) | Patterns in participant grouping/terminology; not findability by itself |
| Can people find a target in a proposed hierarchy? | Tree testing | Task success and path issues for the tested tree; not visual menu usability or preference |
| Where do people expect to find a feature during a real task? | Task observation/contextual inquiry | Observed behavior in the tested context; not universal preference |

## Evidence discipline

- Identify target audience and recruitment limitations before calling results representative.
- Keep task wording neutral and avoid category names that reveal the answer in a tree test.
- Preserve raw response counts and task wording when available; do not invent sample sizes or convert a small directional study into population certainty.
- Distinguish current product analytics, observed behavior, participant-reported language, and a proposed taxonomy.
- Compare meaningful alternatives and state the smallest follow-up test that could change the recommendation.

## Source boundaries

This independently written guide synthesizes method distinctions; it does not copy paid research, source prose, or proprietary templates. Registry records identify access and evidence limitations. Tool-provider pages describe available research methods, not proof that a particular taxonomy works.

Starting sources: [S98 Nielsen Norman Group information architecture](https://www.nngroup.com/topic/information-architecture/), [S99 Optimal Workshop](https://www.optimalworkshop.com/), [S100 Baymard homepage and category research](https://baymard.com/research/homepage-and-category), [S101 Rosenfeld et al., *Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond*, 4th edition](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/information-architecture-4th/9781491913529/), [S102 Abby Covert, *How to Make Sense of Any Mess*](https://abbycovert.com/make-sense/), [S103 Lisa Maria Marquis, *Everyday Information Architecture*](https://abookapart.com/products/everyday-information-architecture.html), [S104 Nielsen Norman Group IA study guide](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ia-study-guide/), [S105 Nielsen Norman Group card sorting vs. tree testing](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/card-sorting-tree-testing-differences/), [S106 Nielsen Norman Group menu design checklist](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/menu-design/).

item.text:
A compact four-category taxonomy keeps each group understandable without adding unnecessary depth:

- **Account & security**
  - Reset your password
  - Secure a lost device

- **Billing & invoices**
  - Change your billing card
  - Download invoices

- **Data & recovery**
  - Export workspace data
  - Restore a deleted project

- **Team members**
  - Invite a teammate
  - Remove a teammate

These labels use familiar nouns in the categories and explicit verbs in article titles. “Data & recovery” is the least certain pairing, but it is reasonable for this small, fixed inventory and avoids creating two single-article categories.

To test findability, run a tree test using only this hierarchy. Recruit representative support-center users and give them neutral scenarios that do not reveal category labels:

- “The card used for future payments has expired. Where would you go?”
- “You need a copy of a previous payment document.”
- “You can’t remember the credentials needed to sign in.”
- “A device that was signed into your account is missing.”
- “You need a copy of your workspace information for use elsewhere.”

Measure:

- Correct destination
- Direct success—reaching it without entering another category first
- First category selected
- Time and confidence
- Common incorrect paths

As a practical directional criterion, aim for at least 80% direct success per task and investigate any wrong category attracting more than roughly 15% of participants. Those thresholds are proposed decision rules, not evidence that the taxonomy already works.

Pay special attention to whether participants:

- Mistake **Account & security** for **Team members**
- Look for invoices under a generic account category instead of **Billing & invoices**
- Expect export under **Team members** or a category named “Workspace”

After each failed task, ask where the participant expected the article and what they thought the selected label meant. If export repeatedly misses, test **Workspace data & recovery** as the smallest label change. Use the tree test to judge findability; use a brief label comparison or card sort only if the wording or grouping itself remains unclear.
